k: Forgetfulness is excused — "Our Lord, do not hold us accountable if we forget or err" (Quran {1}). A man came to the Prophet ﷺ at Ji'ranah in a perfumed cloak; he was told to wash off the perfume and take the cloak off — nothing more (Bukhari {2}). Stop the act, remove the cause, carry on. Scholars differ on the fidyah: for perfume or clothing used through genuine forgetfulness or ignorance the Shafi'is and Hanbalis say nothing is due (this hadith is their evidence), while the Hanafis and Malikis generally still require one, and most scholars require one for cutting hair or nails, or hunting, even by mistake — ask a scholar.

Fully valid. The upper floors and the mataf ring circle the same House, and the Prophet ﷺ himself performed tawaf mounted on a camel (Bukhari {1}). Free wheelchair services and paid pushers are available — ask the Haram staff near the gates.

If you can, go back to the miqat and enter ihram there. If not, enter ihram where you are, <1>complete your Umrah or Hajj — it is valid</1> — and ask a scholar afterwards about the dam (a sheep slaughtered in the Haram) that most scholars require for crossing the miqat without ihram. Do not abandon your Umrah or Hajj over this.

It counts and it is rewarded: a woman lifted up a child and asked, "Is there Hajj for this one?" — "Yes, and you will have a reward" (Sahih Muslim). A child's Hajj does not fulfil the obligatory Hajj of Islam: the scholars agree it must be performed again after puberty (at-Tirmidhi, after hadith {1}). A <1>discerning child</1> (roughly {2}+) makes his or her own intention and does the rites; for a <2>young child</2> the guardian makes the intention on their behalf, carries or leads them round, and keeps them from the ihram prohibitions as far as a parent reasonably can. Whether one tawaf counts for both carrier and child is disputed: the Hanafis, and scholars such as Ibn Baz and al-Sa'di, say it counts for both when intended for both, while many Shafi'i and Hanbali scholars say it counts for only one of you — a separate tawaf for each is the safer course if you can manage it (ask if unsure). Boys shave or trim; girls trim. Resting, feeding and nappy changes are fine — see "Can I rest?" above.

No — "Tawaf around the House is like salah, except that you speak during it; so whoever speaks in it, let him say only good." (Tirmidhi {1}). Necessary talk is fine; idle chatter and phone-scrolling waste a moment you may never get back.

No — both are sunnah for men in the arrival tawaf (Hanafis and Shafi'is: also in a later tawaf followed by sa'i). Skipping them (crowds, weakness, forgetting) affects nothing. The obligations of tawaf include: purity, covering the awrah, seven complete rounds around the House, keeping the Kaaba on your left, and starting from the Black Stone (required by the Malikis, Shafi'is and Hanbalis).

No — the requirement for men is an izar and rida not tailored to the body (a hem, seam or patch is fine); clean is expected, white is recommended, new is not required. Washing your ihram or changing into a spare set while in ihram is perfectly fine. For women, any modest clothing in any colour is their ihram.

Renew your wudu and return. The Hanafis and Shafi'is hold you build on what you completed — resume from where you stopped, or repeat that round to be safe; the Malikis and the Hanbali school hold the tawaf restarts from the beginning, which is the safer course if you are able. Crowding makes this common — no panic, it does not ruin your Umrah or Hajj.

She assumes ihram at the miqat like everyone (ihram does not require purity), keeps up the talbiyah, dhikr and dua, and <1>delays tawaf — and the sa'i after it — until she is pure</1> (Bukhari {1}). Full guidance, incl. the farewell tawaf and what to do if the flight comes first:
Trim, never shave (Abu Dawud {1}); talbiyah softly; no raml, no jogging.

Yes — <1>badal Umrah</1> for a deceased person, or one permanently unable (chronic illness, old age), is held by the majority (the Malikis disapprove of it for a living person): the Prophet ﷺ told a man whose father was too old to travel, "Perform Hajj and Umrah on behalf of your father" (Abu Dawud {1}), and when he heard a man saying "Labbayk on behalf of Shubrumah" he told him to perform Hajj for himself first, then for Shubrumah (Abu Dawud {2}). So: your own Umrah first, then on behalf of others — one person per Umrah.

Yes — you may pause to rest, drink Zamzam, or pray an obligatory prayer when the iqamah is called, then continue from where you left off. The rites are acts of devotion, not endurance tests: "Allah intends for you ease" (Quran {1}).

Yes, if you genuinely cannot go: illness, old age, pregnancy, disability, a small child, or real fear of the crush. Jabir (RA): "we recited the talbiyah on behalf of the children and stoned the pillars on their behalf" (agreed fiqh — Ibn Majah {1} has a weak chain, its meaning is accepted); scholars extend this to any adult unable to go (Malikis add a dam for the adult who is unable). Rules of thumb: the proxy should have <1>stoned for themselves first</1> that day (or throw yours jamarah by jamarah after their own); they say the takbir with each pebble as usual; you make dua where you are. Finding it merely tiring is not an excuse — most scholars allow the night hours for those who could not go in the day (the Hanbali school: the next day after midday), and the bridge is quieter then. Tell your group leader; most groups organise proxies for the elderly. Ask a scholar if you are unsure whether your reason counts.

Yes. The Prophet ﷺ ordered 'Abdur-Rahman to take his sister Aishah (RA) to <1>Tan'eem (Masjid Aisha)</1> to perform an Umrah from there (Bukhari {1}). Exit the Haram boundary, assume a fresh ihram, and repeat the rites. Scholars differ on how much repetition is ideal — quality and khushu come before quantity.

Around the Haramain you will meet rehearsed stories: a mother with a sleeping baby (sometimes rented for the day), "my wallet was stolen and I need a ticket home", "my child needs surgery", a shown photo of a sick relative. Organised gangs run many of these, and they target pilgrims whose hearts are soft after worship. <1>Your mercy is not naive — but your money should be smart:</1> give through Ehsan, your trusted charity at home, or to people whose situation you actually know. Begging is illegal in the Haramain; report persistent cases to security rather than engaging.

Don't argue with scammers — walk away and report: any Haram security officer, the police at <1>{1}</1>, or the Ministry of Hajj & Umrah care line <2>{2}</2>. Reporting protects the pilgrims who come after you. And if you were fooled — your intention was charity, and "actions are but by intentions" (Bukhari {3}): your reward is with Allah; get wiser, not colder.

Men near the mataf offering — for a fee — to "get you to the Black Stone", into the Rawdah, or a "private tawaf". The Rawdah is a free Nusuk permit; the Black Stone is reached by patience or pointed to from afar, as the Prophet ﷺ did (Bukhari {1}); there is no private tawaf. Paying touts funds harassment of pilgrims and usually buys nothing.

Online services take payment to perform Umrah or Hajj "on behalf of your deceased parents" — and many simply pocket the money; you have no way to verify anything happened. If you want badal for a loved one, arrange it through <1>someone you personally know and trust</1> — for a badal Hajj, someone who has already performed their own Hajj — or, for a badal Umrah, do it yourself from Tan'eem while you're there. Reward cannot be bought from a webshop.

People with card readers or printed QR codes collecting for "mosque construction", "orphans" or "Quran printing" in streets and hotel lobbies. Unregulated collection is illegal in Saudi Arabia precisely because of fraud. Scan nothing. Your sadaqah does more through <1><2>Ehsan (ehsan.sa)</2></1>, your home mosque, or a charity whose registration you can check.

Scammers clone the Nusuk website and app to harvest passport details, card numbers and OTP codes. <1>Only use <2>nusuk.sa</2> / <3>umrah.nusuk.sa</3></1> typed directly, or the app from the official Apple/Google stores. Never share an OTP with anyone — no real official will ever ask. Never hand your passport to a "helper" you just met.

The Rawdah visit permit and the Umrah permit are <1>free on the Nusuk app</1>, and a Hajj permit comes only with a licensed Hajj package. Anyone selling you a "permit", "slot" or "VIP access" is selling you nothing. And in Saudi Arabia, collecting donations in streets and mosques is <2>illegal outside official platforms</2> — the Kingdom's official donation platform is <3><4>Ehsan (ehsan.sa)</4></3>. When in doubt: if it isn't Nusuk or Ehsan, walk away politely.
